practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a child should travel in a rear-facing car seat until they are at least 15 months old.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the reason (e.g. 'rear-facing seats provide better protection in a frontal collision'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'because in a frontal crash the seat absorbs and spreads the impact force across the baby's back, head and neck together'). A third mark for a further linked point (e.g. 'young infants have disproportionately large and heavy heads relative to their neck muscles, making them vulnerable to serious head and spinal injury in a forward-facing seat during a collision; rear-facing seats significantly reduce this risk'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the UKCA mark and the BSI Kitemark. Give one example of a product on which a parent might look for these marks.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the UKCA mark is the legal minimum conformity marking indicating a product meets UK safety law requirements; the BSI Kitemark is a voluntary mark awarded by the British Standards Institution confirming the product has been independently tested to the relevant British Standard — providing a higher level of assurance than the UKCA mark alone (2 marks for a clear distinction covering legal status and level of testing; 1 mark for a basic distinction only).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, when buying a stair gate, a parent should look for the BSI Kitemark confirming it has been tested to BS EN 1930, giving greater confidence in the gate's strength and reliability than the basic UKCA mark alone (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example such as 'toys' without development). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Priya is decorating her home ready for the arrival of her first child. She wants to make both the living room and the kitchen as safe as possible for when the baby begins crawling and walking.

Discuss the safety measures Priya should take in her home to reduce the risk of accidents to her child.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two types of hazard in the relevant rooms (e.g. living room — socket covers or child-resistant sockets, corner and edge protectors on furniture, securing heavy furniture to walls, keeping cables tidy, fireguard on any open fire; kitchen — stair gate across door, cooker guard, turning pan handles inward, storing cleaning products in locked cupboard, keeping hot drinks out of reach) with specific prevention measures for each, and acknowledging limits (e.g. making an environment fully safe may not be feasible; supervision remains essential alongside physical safety measures; risks change as the child develops and new hazards emerge).
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant hazards identified with prevention measures, some reference to Priya's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One or two hazards with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Despite significant improvements in home safety products and public awareness campaigns, accidental injury remains the leading cause of death among children aged 1–14 in the UK.

Evaluate how effectively safety equipment and safety standards can reduce the risk of accidental injury to young children.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Evaluates specific equipment and its effectiveness (stair gates prevent stair falls; socket covers prevent electrocution; cooker guards and thermostat settings reduce scald risk; car seats reduce road fatality) and how safety standards (UKCA, BSI Kitemark, i-Size) ensure products are rigorously tested. Argues that these measures have demonstrably reduced specific accident types. Challenges this with evidence that equipment alone is insufficient — supervision is always required (a stair gate left open is useless; a child can still drown in 5 cm of water in a supervised moment); some safety products can give a false sense of security; lower-income families may be unable to afford high-quality safety equipment; accidents still occur because children's behaviour is unpredictable and hazard awareness changes with development. Reaches a substantiated judgement — for example, that safety equipment and standards are highly effective in reducing specific, predictable hazards but must be combined with active supervision and parental education to address the full range of risks, particularly as children become more mobile and independently exploratory.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more developed points on each side with an attempted conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but mainly one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

A voluntary UK quality and safety mark awarded by the British Standards Institution, indicating a product has been independently tested to the relevant British Standard.
